scenario: AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

While a religious community may provide a sense of belonging, moral guidance, and a shared set of values, a group of people you respect and share values with can indeed have a similar positive impact on individuals. This type of group, often referred to as a "secular community" or "values-based community," can provide a supportive environment that encourages personal growth and self-improvement. Here are some reasons why a values-based community can be just as effective as a religious community in pushing people to be better: 1. **Shared values and goals**: When you surround yourself with people who share your values and goals, you're more likely to feel motivated and inspired to work towards them. This shared sense of purpose can create a sense of accountability and encourage individuals to strive for personal growth. 2. **Supportive environment**: A values-based community can provide a safe and supportive space for individuals to discuss their challenges, share their experiences, and learn from one another. This environment can foster a sense of trust, empathy, and understanding, which can be just as powerful as the sense of community found in a religious setting. 3. **Role models and mentors**: When you surround yourself with people you respect and admire, you're more likely to be inspired by their examples and motivated to emulate their positive qualities. This can be especially true if you have a mentor or role model within the group who can offer guidance and support. 4. **Accountability and encouragement**: A values-based community can provide a sense of accountability, where individuals feel motivated to live up to the expectations of their peers. This can be a powerful driver of personal growth, as individuals strive to meet the standards set by their community. 5. **Flexibility and autonomy**: Unlike a religious community, a values-based community may offer more flexibility and autonomy, allowing individuals to explore their own spirituality and values without feeling bound by dogma or doctrine. However, it's worth noting that a values-based community may not provide the same level of structure and guidance as a religious community. Without a clear set of rules or teachings, individuals may need to take more responsibility for their own personal growth and development. Ultimately, whether a values-based community can push people to be better in the same way a religious community does depends on the specific individuals involved and the values they share.
